segments.source: For this classroom model, Eastport is 1 time zone(s) east of Westport. Each zone east is one hour later. At Westport it is 9:00.
Moving east adds one hour per stated time zone; moving west subtracts. Use the given model only.
What local time is it in Eastport?
1. Time difference is +1 hour(s) because Eastport is east. 2. 9+1=10 (mod 24).

Problem 139. Earth, sunlight, and local time: case 4
Earth–Sun relationships explain broad patterns such as day length and local time, but a problem should state the simplified model it expects children to use.
Use this simplified model: Earth’s axis is tilted. In the Northern Hemisphere, days are generally longer around June than around December. Compare June and December for the same place.
Use the stated seasonal relation; do not infer daily weather from season.
Which of the two months has the longer daylight period in this model, and can that fact alone tell us whether it will rain?
1. Apply the stated tilt-season relation. 2. June has the longer daylight period in the Northern Hemisphere. 3. The rule contains no information about rainfall, so rainfall cannot be deduced.
June has longer daylight; rainfall cannot be determined from this fact alone.

Problem 141. Reservoir stock and flow: case 1
Many geographic and civic quantities are stocks and flows: water in a reservoir, people in a city, or goods in a warehouse.
A reservoir starts with 25 water units. Each day 5 units flow in and 4 units flow out. Assume these rates stay constant for 3 days.
Stock at the end = starting stock + total inflow − total outflow. Flow is an amount per time period; stock is the amount currently stored.
How much water is stored after 3 days? Is the stock increasing or decreasing each day?
1. Daily net change=5−4=1. 2. Over 3 days, net change=3×1=3. 3. End stock=25+(3)=28.
Do not confuse a stored amount with a rate of change; conservation links them.

Problem 146. Density and capacity in a public space: case 1
Density compares an amount with the space available. It can reveal crowding even when two places have similar total populations.
A park zone covers 4 hectares and currently has 25 visitors. For this exercise, comfortable density is at most 6 visitors per hectare.
Density = number ÷ area. A zone exceeds comfortable capacity if density is greater than the stated threshold.
What is the visitor density, and is the zone above the stated comfortable capacity?
1. Density=25÷4=6.25 visitors/hectare. 2. Compare 6.25 with the threshold 6.
Totals and densities answer different questions; always identify the denominator.
Ratio density=N/A followed by threshold comparison.
